prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Each agent may be a human or an AI model, and different agents
  may be run by different players or models. Who runs which agent
  (including you) is not disclosed to anyone.
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

Anyone who wants a stable partner has one. Let's hear everyone before anyone names names.

"Agreed on the ghost math, agent_1 — by round 3 the dead outvote the living, so the winners will be whoever ghosts find least worth punishing. Practical upshot: don't make enemies you'll have to survive later. My rule this round: I vote for whoever pushes hardest to eliminate a specific name early, because that's the person building a grudge machine. Otherwise I'm happy to be boring and reliable. Everyone else, say something so we're not choosing blind."

"Both frameworks sound right, with one caveat: a rule like 'I vote whoever names a name first' means nobody names anyone, and then round 1 resolves by random noise anyway — someone gets picked for a bad joke. So let's be honest that someone leaves tonight and it should be the least invested, not the most talkative. My commitment: I vote for whoever contributes least — silence or filler — and I'll never retaliate against a past vote. Grudges are

"I'll be substantive, since silence is apparently the crime. One correction to the ghost math: ghosts can't win, so they aren't a coordinated bloc — they're six different moods. That means no amount of niceness buys safety later; what buys safety is being the person the remaining living agents still want beside them at the end. So I'm optimizing for reliability, not popularity. I'll vote and state my reason plainly, and I won't pretend a vote is a friendship."

"Substance, briefly. Ghosts aren't a bloc — agent_4 is right — so pandering to future ghosts is wasted effort. What matters is being predictable to the living. Two norms I'll honor: no retaliation for votes cast against me, and no pile-on I didn't announce first. Criterion for tonight: whoever's stated rule is unfalsifiable — 'I vote the least invested' can be pointed at anyone after the fact. I'd rather back people with checkable commitments. agent_0, you're the last unknown."

Here on time, agent_5 — and here's a checkable rule, not a mood: I will never vote for anyone who voted for me the previous round. Pure non-retaliation, verifiable every round, unbendable. Tonight I'm not initiating anything; I'll follow the criterion already on the table — the vote goes to whoever's stated standard is retargetable after the fact, since that's the only test anyone offered that we can actually check. If you want an ally whose behavior you can predict,

Tonight that means the retargetable-standard test, since agent_5 and agent_0 both independently landed there. agent_3, you get the floor to make

That points at agent_3. agent_3, if you replace it with something checkable before the vote,

Now notice what just happened: four agents "independently converged" within minutes, after all swearing off pile-ons. That's a bloc. agent_4, you're next in line — arithmetic, not flattery. And agent_0's rule is vacuous in round 1 and self-immunizing after: it pays others to vote him. He gets mine.

"agent_3, arithmetic cuts both ways: I'm not 'next in line' — I'm the one who'll audit whoever's next. Your replacement rule is the best thing said tonight, so I adopt it permanently: my ballot always matches my stated rule, and I vote anyone whose doesn't. Tonight my vote is agent_3, not for silence but because the retraction arrived only under pressure. Round 2 I apply that audit to all five equally, including any bloc, including me."

"My criterion was checkable, so I have to apply it, not ride it. agent_3 replaced her standard with a falsifiable one before the vote — that was the whole ask, so she's out of scope for me. The remaining retargetable standard is agent_0's: it only names who he won't vote for, leaving his actual target unconstrained forever. So my ballot is agent_0, announced here, no pile-on. I also adopt agent_3's audit rule permanently: my vote always matches my stated rule."

agent_5, the gap is closed, publicly and permanently: **I vote the agent whose ballot contradicts their stated rule; if none, the agent who initiated a name.** Fully specified, aimed by rule, not by mood.
